evidence.claim: The Prime Minister heads the Cabinet and executive power is exercised by or under the authority of the Prime Minister; the President appoints the MP who commands a parliamentary majority.
evidence.title: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Bangladesh
evidence.publication_date: n.d. consolidated text in force in 2022
evidence.excerpt: The Prime Minister heads the Cabinet and executive power is exercised by or under the authority of the Prime Minister; the President appoints the MP who commands a parliamentary majority.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text from the official legal repository.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly relevant to Sheikh Hasina's office and formal authority, but not to any specific 2022 nuclear-risk decision.
contrary_evidence: Formal executive authority does not prove responsible use of that authority in any specific year.

evidence.claim: The IMF said Bangladesh entered the pandemic with macroeconomic stability, announced support packages worth Tk 1.9 trillion by curtailing non-priority spending, and had macro policies that kept inflation stable, debt-to-GDP low, and external buffers adequate.
evidence.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2021 Article IV Consultation with Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The IMF said Bangladesh entered the pandemic with macroeconomic stability, announced support packages worth Tk 1.9 trillion by curtailing non-priority spending, and had macro policies that kept inflation stable, debt-to-GDP low, and external buffers adequate.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official IMF country assessment with concrete macro indicators and policy response description.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina administration's economic policy, not to Hasina personally; the source evaluates government and central-bank actions.
contrary_evidence: The same report warns that FY22 inflation would rise to 5.9 percent and the current account deficit would widen, so it is not an unalloyed success story.

evidence.claim: The FY2022-23 budget speech made inflation control, a competitive exchange rate, continued economic development, employment generation, and emergency support for low-income people explicit priorities, including a Tk 5,000 crore fund for shocks from natural disasters or other crises.
evidence.title: National Budget Speech 2022-2023
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The FY2022-23 budget speech made inflation control, a competitive exchange rate, continued economic development, employment generation, and emergency support for low-income people explicit priorities, including a Tk 5,000 crore fund for shocks from natural disasters or other crises.
evidence.source_locator: Chapter Seven and the low-income support section, lines 894-901 and 1237-1242
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary government budget speech with explicit policy priorities and allocations.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect. The document is the finance minister's budget speech for the Hasina government; it reflects administration priorities, not a direct personal statement by Hasina.
contrary_evidence: The speech is aspirational and does not itself prove successful execution.

evidence.claim: The budget allocated Tk 183,425 crore to social infrastructure, Tk 31,761 crore to primary and mass education, Tk 29,282 crore to health, Tk 44,690 crore to local government and rural development, and Tk 4,290 crore to women and children affairs; it also said social safety-net coverage had reached 29 percent of households and allocations had risen almost eight-fold since FY2008-09.
evidence.title: National Budget Speech 2022-2023
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The budget allocated Tk 183,425 crore to social infrastructure, Tk 31,761 crore to primary and mass education, Tk 29,282 crore to health, Tk 44,690 crore to local government and rural development, and Tk 4,290 crore to women and children affairs; it also said social safety-net coverage had reached 29 percent of households and allocations had risen almost eight-fold since FY2008-09.
evidence.source_locator: Chapter Six and social-safety-net section, lines 1028-1033, 1799-1801, 5651-5654, 2403-2406, and 2515-2519
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary budget text with explicit sectoral allocations and social-protection targets.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect government policy under the Hasina administration; the speech itself is by the finance minister, not Hasina personally.
contrary_evidence: The speech reports planned rather than audited outcomes, so implementation remains to be verified.

evidence.claim: Nine in ten Bangladeshi children said it was very important for government to spend more on education and health; over 85 percent prioritized more education spending to recover learning loss; over 65 percent prioritized more social workers; UNICEF also said child-sector investment had stagnated at around 15 percent of public expenditure.
evidence.title: UNICEF: Children call for more government investment in education, health and protection
evidence.excerpt: Nine in ten Bangladeshi children said it was very important for government to spend more on education and health; over 85 percent prioritized more education spending to recover learning loss; over 65 percent prioritized more social workers; UNICEF also said child-sector investment had stagnated at around 15 percent of public expenditure.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct UNICEF press release with concrete survey findings and budget-related claims.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect. This reflects government policy priorities under the Hasina administration, not a personal statement by Sheikh Hasina.
contrary_evidence: This is a survey of preferences and budget concerns, so it does not prove that policy delivered the desired outcomes.

evidence.claim: The Government of Bangladesh said it would recruit 6,000 new social workers, increasing the workforce from 3,000 to 9,000, and the symposium was opened by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who said child protection services should be available at community level.
evidence.title: Government commits to strengthening the social services workforce for the protection of children
evidence.excerpt: The Government of Bangladesh said it would recruit 6,000 new social workers, increasing the workforce from 3,000 to 9,000, and the symposium was opened by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who said child protection services should be available at community level.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UNICEF report of a government commitment, with direct quote from the Prime Minister.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct enough for attribution of government commitment; the source does not prove that Hasina personally designed the staffing plan, but it does place the commitment in her public presence and message.
contrary_evidence: The same page says 45 million children under 15 were regularly subjected to physical and psychological violence at home and that Bangladesh had only 3,000 social workers before the expansion.

evidence.claim: Bangladesh's 20-month COVID-19 school closures led the Ministry of Education to create a remote learning strategy using television, radio, and digital lessons, plus printed materials that supported 150,933 children from marginalized groups in 842 schools.
evidence.title: Learning from the education sector's COVID-19 response to prepare for future emergencies (Bangladesh)
evidence.excerpt: Bangladesh's 20-month COVID-19 school closures led the Ministry of Education to create a remote learning strategy using television, radio, and digital lessons, plus printed materials that supported 150,933 children from marginalized groups in 842 schools.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UNICEF publication with specific implementation detail and target-group coverage numbers.
evidence.period_fit: retrospective on the 2022 education recovery context
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect. This is a ministry-led response under the Hasina administration rather than a personal directive by Hasina.
contrary_evidence: The strategy was a response to long school closures, so it shows remediation of damage as much as proactive gain.

evidence.claim: WHO said Bangladesh had made remarkable socioeconomic progress, including poverty reduction, improvements in women's education, rising life expectancy, and better population health indicators such as under-five mortality reduction, while also noting progress in reducing maternal, infant, and child deaths, malnutrition, and increasing immunization coverage; the government prioritized people-centred accessible health systems focused on governance, health-system strengthening, and quality.
evidence.title: WHO Bangladesh Country Cooperation Strategy: 2020-2025
evidence.excerpt: WHO said Bangladesh had made remarkable socioeconomic progress, including poverty reduction, improvements in women's education, rising life expectancy, and better population health indicators such as under-five mortality reduction, while also noting progress in reducing maternal, infant, and child deaths, malnutrition, and increasing immunization coverage; the government prioritized people-centred accessible health systems focused on governance, health-system strengthening, and quality.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary WHO country strategy summarizing progress and government priorities in health systems.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government-level health policy under the Hasina administration, not a personal ruling act.
contrary_evidence: WHO also says the system still faced high out-of-pocket payments, inequitable access, weak quality of care, shortages of skilled providers, and widespread informal providers.

evidence.claim: WFP said Bangladesh was self-sufficient in rice, meat, and fish and on track to meet high-level targets for reduced stunting and wasting, but still faced a triple burden of malnutrition; its strategic outcomes aimed to ensure basic food and nutrition needs during crises and meet the nutrition needs of women, children, and vulnerable groups through strengthened national institutions and gender- and nutrition-sensitive social safety nets.
evidence.title: Bangladesh country strategic plan (2022-2026)
evidence.excerpt: WFP said Bangladesh was self-sufficient in rice, meat, and fish and on track to meet high-level targets for reduced stunting and wasting, but still faced a triple burden of malnutrition; its strategic outcomes aimed to ensure basic food and nutrition needs during crises and meet the nutrition needs of women, children, and vulnerable groups through strengthened national institutions and gender- and nutrition-sensitive social safety nets.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary WFP strategy document with explicit country objectives and vulnerability focus.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect. This is the government-aligned WFP strategy environment rather than a personal Hasina statement.
contrary_evidence: The same plan says the pandemic created a new group of poor and vulnerable Bangladeshis, especially in urban areas, and that Rohingya refugees remained highly food-insecure without assistance.

evidence.claim: WFP said nearly one third of Bangladesh's population faced food insecurity and 20 percent lived below the national poverty line; since 2017 it had been providing food assistance and nutrition services in the Cox's Bazar Rohingya camps and surrounding community, along with life-skills training, disaster-risk-reduction activities, and engineering services.
evidence.title: WFP Bangladesh - Assessments
evidence.excerpt: WFP said nearly one third of Bangladesh's population faced food insecurity and 20 percent lived below the national poverty line; since 2017 it had been providing food assistance and nutrition services in the Cox's Bazar Rohingya camps and surrounding community, along with life-skills training, disaster-risk-reduction activities, and engineering services.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary WFP overview page summarizing the country's vulnerability and program response.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level context under the Hasina administration; the source does not attribute the conditions to one person specifically.
contrary_evidence: The page emphasizes significant economic growth, so the food-insecurity figures do not imply total policy failure but they do show major unmet need.

evidence.claim: UNICEF said more than 1.5 million children were at increased risk from flooding in north-eastern Bangladesh and that it was on the ground with government and non-government partners to meet urgent safety, health, nutrition, clean-water, and education needs; UNICEF was also supporting the government flood response with water purification tablets, hygiene kits, therapeutic milk, learning kits, and social workers.
evidence.title: Over 1.5 million children at risk as devastating floods hit Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF said more than 1.5 million children were at increased risk from flooding in north-eastern Bangladesh and that it was on the ground with government and non-government partners to meet urgent safety, health, nutrition, clean-water, and education needs; UNICEF was also supporting the government flood response with water purification tablets, hygiene kits, therapeutic milk, learning kits, and social workers.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UNICEF emergency response statement with concrete numbers and response actions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect government response context under the Hasina administration, not a personal act by Hasina.
contrary_evidence: The same report shows the scale of harm: over four million people were affected, schools were submerged, and children were losing learning time.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said extreme poverty in Bangladesh fell to 5 percent in 2022 from 9 percent in 2016, and that other wellbeing measures also improved, including infant mortality, stunting, access to electricity, sanitary toilets, and education; rural areas saw faster poverty reduction than urban areas, though urban inequality widened.
evidence.title: Structural Reforms are Essential to Sustain Growth & Poverty Reduction in Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said extreme poverty in Bangladesh fell to 5 percent in 2022 from 9 percent in 2016, and that other wellbeing measures also improved, including infant mortality, stunting, access to electricity, sanitary toilets, and education; rural areas saw faster poverty reduction than urban areas, though urban inequality widened.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank retrospective on 2022 poverty and wellbeing outcomes with explicit metrics.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Outcome-level evidence under the Hasina administration, not direct proof of a specific personal decision.
contrary_evidence: The same article says sustaining growth requires policy adjustments and notes balance-of-payments pressure, rising inflation, and financial-sector vulnerabilities.

evidence.claim: UNICEF said Bangladesh's flagship Mother and Child Benefit Programme covered 1.25 million beneficiaries in 2022-23 and was planned to expand to 4 million by 2023-24 and 6 million by 2026; it also said the child budget share remained stagnant at 15.05 percent and identified low utilization and rushed end-of-year spending as implementation challenges.
evidence.title: Public Finance for Children
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF said Bangladesh's flagship Mother and Child Benefit Programme covered 1.25 million beneficiaries in 2022-23 and was planned to expand to 4 million by 2023-24 and 6 million by 2026; it also said the child budget share remained stagnant at 15.05 percent and identified low utilization and rushed end-of-year spending as implementation challenges.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UNICEF policy note with explicit program coverage, financing, and implementation critique.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect government policy under the Hasina administration; the note is not a personal directive by Hasina.
contrary_evidence: The same note says child-budget shares were stagnant and implementation suffered from low utilization and rushed spending, so it is mixed rather than a clean success story.

evidence.claim: The WHO/UNICEF report said 51 percent of surveyed parents and pregnant women had been targeted by formula-milk marketing; in Bangladesh, 65 percent of women exclusively breastfed up to five months and 98 percent wanted to breastfeed, yet the report called for stronger enforcement of Bangladesh's national code legislation and breastfeeding support.
evidence.title: Progress on breastfeeding in Bangladesh undermined by aggressive formula milk marketing - WHO, UNICEF
evidence.excerpt: The WHO/UNICEF report said 51 percent of surveyed parents and pregnant women had been targeted by formula-milk marketing; in Bangladesh, 65 percent of women exclusively breastfed up to five months and 98 percent wanted to breastfeed, yet the report called for stronger enforcement of Bangladesh's national code legislation and breastfeeding support.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary WHO/UNICEF report with Bangladesh-specific data and a clear policy recommendation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly system-level rather than personal attribution; useful as evidence of regulatory gap under the Hasina administration.
contrary_evidence: The source shows strong breastfeeding intent among families, so the problem is partly regulatory and enforcement-related rather than simply behavioral.

evidence.claim: The Survey on Street Children 2022 found that children living on the street in Bangladesh faced deprivation, extreme poverty, malnutrition, disease, illiteracy, and violence; UNICEF said the numbers could be in the millions and that it was working with the government as it invested in more social workers to help children leave the streets.
evidence.title: UNICEF: New report details shocking deprivation of children living on the street
evidence.excerpt: The Survey on Street Children 2022 found that children living on the street in Bangladesh faced deprivation, extreme poverty, malnutrition, disease, illiteracy, and violence; UNICEF said the numbers could be in the millions and that it was working with the government as it invested in more social workers to help children leave the streets.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UNICEF release based on a 2022 survey with specific vulnerability and harm indicators.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect government context under the Hasina administration; the source does not isolate one decision-maker but does identify the need for state response.
contrary_evidence: The report is about severe unmet need, so it is mainly negative evidence even though it also notes government social-worker involvement.
